plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a two-lens telescope system consisting of a convex objective lens (lens 1, on the left) and a concave eyepiece lens (lens 2, on the right), with the distances f1 and f2 indicated by horizontal brackets beneath the optical axis. Two parallel input rays enter from the left at a small angle δᵢ relative to the optical axis; lens 1 bends them toward the objective focal point to the right of lens 2, and lens 2 then diverges the rays so they exit as a parallel bundle at a larger angle δₒ. The blue vertical marker d shows the offset of the shared focal point from the optical axis in the shown Galilean afocal geometry, where the objective focal point aligns with the eyepiece focal point. This figure demonstrates how a Galilean-style telescope achieves angular magnification equal to the ratio f1/f2 by manipulating ray angles through the two-lens arrangement.

interactionPlan.concept: A Galilean two-lens telescope converts a small incoming ray angle into a larger outgoing parallel ray angle, with angular magnification set by the focal-length ratio f1/f2 when the lenses are in the afocal separation.
elements: horizontal optical axis drawn as a thin blue line
convex objective lens on the left, labeled 'lens 1'
concave eyepiece lens on the right, labeled 'lens 2'
two incoming parallel purple rays entering from the left at angle δi to the optical axis
curved angle markers at the left showing δi for the incoming ray direction
purple ray segments refracted by lens 1 toward the shared off-axis focal point
purple ray segments passing through lens 2 and emerging to the right
two outgoing parallel purple rays leaving at a larger angle δo to the optical axis in the afocal case
curved angle marker at the right showing δo for the outgoing ray direction
dotted purple construction ray showing the would-be continuation toward the shared focal point
blue vertical offset marker d from the optical axis to the off-axis focal point
blue point on the optical axis above the offset marker
purple point or ray intersection marking the off-axis focal point
horizontal bracket labeled f1 from lens 1 to the shared focal point position
horizontal bracket labeled f2 from lens 2 to the shared focal point position
real-time readout of angular magnification δo/δi = f1/f2
warning/readout for non-afocal lens 2 positions showing converging, parallel, or diverging exit beam

interactions.label: Objective focal length f1
interactions.teaches: A longer objective focal length increases angular magnification because the same incoming angle creates a larger off-axis focal displacement before the eyepiece

interactions.label: Eyepiece focal length f2
interactions.teaches: A shorter eyepiece focal length increases angular magnification because it turns the same focal-plane offset into a steeper outgoing angle
Changing the incoming angle changes both the off-axis focal displacement d and the outgoing angle, while their ratio stays fixed by f1/f2 in the afocal configuration
Only when lens 2 is placed so its focal point coincides with the objective focal point do the exiting rays become parallel; moving it away makes the telescope no longer afocal

demo_steps.title: Afocal telescope setup
demo_steps.narration: Lens 2 is positioned so the focal point of lens 1 coincides with the focal point of lens 2. The incoming parallel bundle exits as another parallel bundle, but at a larger angle.

demo_steps.title: Magnification from focal-length ratio
demo_steps.narration: With f1 = 8 and f2 = 2, the angular magnification readout shows δo/δi = 4. The telescope multiplies angles without needing the rays to form a final real image in the diagram.

demo_steps.title: Lengthen the objective
demo_steps.narration: Increasing f1 moves the shared focal point farther from lens 1 and increases the offset d for the same incoming angle. The outgoing angle grows because the focal-length ratio f1/f2 grows.

demo_steps.title: Shorten the eyepiece
demo_steps.narration: Reducing f2 makes lens 2 convert the same focal offset into an even larger outgoing angle. The lens separation adjusts to maintain the Galilean afocal condition f1 - f2.

demo_steps.title: Break the afocal condition
demo_steps.narration: Now drag lens 2 along the optical axis. When it is not at the afocal separation, the outgoing rays are no longer parallel, showing why the focal points must align.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The telescope magnifies angles because lens 1 converts the incoming angle into a focal-plane offset, and lens 2 converts that same offset back into a larger outgoing angle set by f1/f2.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a wide horizontal SVG layout. Place a tall black convex objective lens left of center and a shorter black concave eyepiece to its right. Draw the optical axis as a thin blue horizontal line. Draw two purple incoming rays from the left, parallel and slightly tilted; one ray may be thicker to emphasize the main construction ray. After lens 1, bend the rays toward an off-axis focal point to the right of lens 2, then through lens 2 so they exit parallel in the default afocal state. Show δi at the left with small curved arrows and δo at the right with a curved arrow. Use blue for the optical-axis reference and the vertical offset marker d, and purple for all light rays and construction rays. The f1 bracket should span from lens 1 to the shared focal point position; the f2 bracket should span from lens 2 to that same point. When f1 or f2 changes, keep lens 2 at the Galilean afocal separation by default and update the displayed magnification ratio. When lens 2 is dragged away from that position, visibly change the exiting rays from parallel to converging or diverging and update the focal-point alignment cue.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Sliders for focal lengths f₁ and f₂: update all ray paths through both lenses and display the angular magnification ratio δₒ/δᵢ = f₁/f₂ in real time, with the lens separation adjusting to maintain the shown Galilean afocal configuration
- Drag the input ray angle δᵢ to change the angle of the two parallel input rays and see the output angle δₒ change proportionally, with ray traces updating through both lenses
- Drag lens 2 along the optical axis to deviate from the shown afocal separation (f₁ - f₂, using the positive bracketed distances), showing the exit beam become converging or diverging and the blue focal-point offset d shift relative to lens 2

authoredPrompt: This figure shows a two-lens telescope system consisting of a convex objective lens (lens 1, on the left) and a concave eyepiece lens (lens 2, on the right), with the distances f1 and f2 indicated by horizontal brackets beneath the optical axis. Two parallel input rays enter from the left at a small angle δᵢ relative to the optical axis; lens 1 bends them toward the objective focal point to the right of lens 2, and lens 2 then diverges the rays so they exit as a parallel bundle at a larger angle δₒ. authoredInteractions:
- Sliders for focal lengths f₁ and f₂: update all ray paths through both lenses and display the angular magnification ratio δₒ/δᵢ = f₁/f₂ in real time, with the lens separation adjusting to maintain the shown Galilean afocal configuration
- Drag the input ray angle δᵢ to change the angle of the two parallel input rays and see the output angle δₒ change proportionally, with ray traces updating through both lenses

authoredContext: A small change in the input ray angle gives a larger change in the output ray angle. The magnification of the telescope is the ratio, $M$, of the angular deviation of an output ray, $\delta_o$, to the angular deviation of an input ray, $\delta_i$.  Writing the focal point offset, $d$, in terms of the rays passing through the centers of lenses 1 and 2 gives the relation, $M = f_1/f_2$, where $f_1$ and $f_2$ are the respective ray focal lengths.

Increase the size and prominence of the lens, δi, δo, d, f1, and f2 labels to better match the source hierarchy.
Move and enlarge the δo curved arrow/label farther to the right so it matches the source composition more closely.
